Author: @guss77
Content:
It's important to explain how DMCA have set the claim and counter claim process: for YouTube to preserve their "platform immunity" they must forward a claim to the original publisher and give them a deadline to respond. While waiting for response, *the content is allowed to stay up.* The publisher can say "oh sorry" or they can simply not respond - *only then* does DMCA requires the content to be taken down. The publisher can instead "counter claim" asserting that there's no copyright infringement - at which point the platform is supposed to keep the content up and give the complainer the contact details of the publisher, telling them they have to sue to get the content down.
The law is annoying but reasonable and more or less fairly balances the rights of copyright owners and content publishers. It's just YouTube that skews the process so massively in favor of large media corporations.

Author: @xaytana
Content: YouTube's punish-first system won't change until their safe harbor status is threatened.  I would think a federal judge would be competent enough to see where YouTube's system leads if a case like this were to be brought before them.  Not only would YouTube be wasting the court's time and resources, as technically all false claim cases could, and should, be taken to court, but there's also the issue that YouTube is also safe harboring the bad actors producing the false claims, of which the combination of such should reasonably allow a judge to strike the platform's safe harbor status.  Safe harbor has become a double edge sword in that platforms are going way too far out of their own bounds and actively harming people financially.  We need a modern fair use act anyways, DMCA was lobbied for and abused by corporations but it was never built to handle what the internet brought, and now that literally anyone reasonably produces copyrighted works it needs to encompass that as well, and now that fair use claim abuses are on the table there needs to be ways to disallow that with legal repercussions.  What would get the ball rolling with this is to attack the largest online media platform in that they've overstepped bounds, threaten their safe harbor status on that basis, and get them to not only implement a better system but also get the court's attention that something needs to be done about this at the legal level.  Precedent like this is never set over nothing, there needs to be action at some point.

Author: @yetanotherbassdude
Content: Legal action against Bloomberg seems justified at this point, but it's a ultimately a symptom, not the source. Content creators need to band together and file a class action lawsuit against YouTube itself. The system they've created for copyright strikes is so one-sided in favour of the copyright owner that it's actively harming free speech and content creators' legal rights to Fair Use. If that can be proven in court, then it makes YouTube itself complicit in every malicious and false claim made by other big media companies and makes them liable for damages from *every failed copyright strike they've ever done*. If you get them on the hook for that, they'll change the system. Nothing short of that will do anything to change how copyright claims work on the platform. You can't do that by yourself, but I guarantee there are hundreds of content creators out there who'll join in and spread the load. So many channels have posted a "I got a copyright strike that made no sense" video. Find them, and that's your class action. Crowdfund the legal fees and you'll see widespread support from the public too. You made a million dollars on one video just to give Bloomberg the middle finger. Imagine what you can do if you really set your sights high.

Author: @supersat
Content:
Here's the same clip, direct from the White House: https://www.youtube.com/live/ZtVMoko3mSI?t=7025s

There's no way Bloomberg has ANY copyright interests in that clip. Even if you got the clip from Bloomberg's website, they're simply republishing content (likely a US Government work, and thus copyright-free) from another source. There's nothing transformative there.

I would definitely talk to your lawyers about filing a claim with the US Copyright Claims Board. This uses the same mechanism the MAFIAA wanted to expedite lawsuits against file sharers. It explicitly allows for quick adjudication over several copyright claims, including:

"Claims for a declaration of noninfringement of an exclusive right (when a party wants a legal confirmation that its activities will not make it liable for infringement);"

and

"Claims for misrepresentation during the notice and counter-notice process for takedown or reinstatement of material on the internet under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA);"

You can also seek up to $30,000 in monetary damages.

Author: @I_am_Phil_Lee
Content:
The YouTube system could be made fair by simply penalising false and frivolous copyright claims in the amount of lost revenue, plus some proportion to cover YouTube's own costs in making the creator financially whole, with maybe a minimum sum in admin fees to cover fixed costs.
Under such a system, a copyright holder could lodge a complaint by paying the minimum admin fee and making a claim, at which point the content would be suspended, and a provisional strike would be lodged against the creator.
The copyright holder would then have 14 days to provide a legal justification that is sufficient for a legal case, or details of an existing legal case which had been filed.
If they provided one which was glaringly inadequate, or if they failed to provide one at all, the content would be reinstated, the provisional strike removed, the fee would be forfeited, and they would be liable for lost revenue (as best assessed by YouTube based on channel metrics of similar content from the past), plus a punitive element to ensure creators were fully compensated and YouTube reimbursed for the cost of running the system.
If the creator just accepted the claim, the strike would be completed, the content fully removed, and the minimum admin fee would be charged to the creator of the content containing the copyrighted material and repaid to the copyright holder.
If a legal case was entered into, either by the copyright holder or by YouTube on their behalf (using the legal justification provided by the copyright holder), that would need to reach its conclusion before the strike was made complete or removed, and proper costs assigned, ensuring that no innocent party had to bear the cost.
Strikes would last for a calendar year before timing out, and the number of allowable strikes per year would vary according to the number of uploads per year.  Only if education was refused and the number of annual strikes exceeded would the channel be deleted.  Education would allow one additional strike.

Author: @2Fast4Mellow
Content:
DMCA is huge fun. Burger King tried to use it to make an blog post go away about how their new drive-thru system is a big (probably vibe coded) mess and a hacker explained what those security flaws detailed weeks. They claimed trademark infringement and instead of thanking a security researcher, they send within one hour a letter from their lawyers to the researcher.

It is not just that fighting Bloomberg would be hugely time consuming, but lawyers are very expensive. The first any (good) lawyer would ask you is what it is what you want to achieve. The lawyers would than contact the other party and see if they want to settle even before the court system is involved. Your number one claim  would have been the re-instatement of the video, but as it already online again, that one is no longer on the table. You could claim for financial compensation (loss of income) but that one is very tricky. Not all videos receive the same amount of viewers. Before the video was taken down, it already received views. It is very hard to proof in court how many views you have missed. At the same time, Bloomberg lawyers would argue that because of the huge exposure (from mainstream media such as Forbes and Washington Post), the other videos have received additional views already compensating part of the loss income. Even if in the end you would be victorious (hooray!), they most likely would appeal and the fight can take several years to complete. The legal system is a swamp and you find yourself in quicksand before you know it and then you also have to consider the sunken ship fallacy. Because you already spend all this money on this, it is a tiny bit extra to continue, rather than to call it a day. This is how many small businesses eventually go bankrupt. 

As the clip in the video was credited to Bloomberg, you already admitted to using their video, meaning that you agree they have the copyright on the video. Now we get into some murky water as they claim all of their videos need to be licensed (their business model) while you (GN) claim fair use of that clip. Meaning it gets all down to definitions and you are no longer in a black and white world. Think how much effort it took GN to raise a million dollar to make this documentary. Yet for Bloomberg this is chump change. If they set aside 1 million and they can hire 4 lawyers a  250/hr for 1000hrs to bury you in the legal system and they just write it off as a business expense. Than there is another thing to consider, what if you loose? It would set a precedent that fair use does not apply to videos that are available for licensing. For Bloomberg (and other media outlets) that would be as huge win.

As my own lawyer (and friend) so often says, being right and getting proven right in court are two very different things!

Author: @AC-cg4be
Content:
It's nice to see someone else not burn a bridge, but stand on the bridge, say "fuck you", then nuke the bridge from orbit.

As a small business owner, lawsuits are very time consuming and you have to weigh the time versus benefit. It sucks, especially for principled people. 

I can tell you as a small business owner and principled person myself, if you ever read this Steve. . .it's worth it. Even if it costs more than you get. The lawyer I got for a frivolous lawsuit filed against me advised me just to pay the plaintiff and move on. I told him "No. It's the principle of the matter." His reply was "A principled man and his money are easily parted." "That's nice. If people don't fight back and show assholes and bullies that people *will* fight back, shit like this will continue." "Fair enough."

It ended up the plaintiff and their lawyer got torn apart by the judge in court and were ordered to pay their court fees, our court fees, and any other fees. Sure, it cost me $1500, but it was well, well worth it to walk away with principles intact and knowing that the right thing had been done.

Author: @SimonMurrayPhuket
Content:
Anyone company or individual making a false or deliberate use of the copyright strike to "punish" or try to financially try to gain from copyright striking a channel SHOULD be punished appropriately if:
1. A false copyright strike is made and is not followed through and proven that the strike was valid.
2. Any financial loss (can be estimated or a fixed fee) through a false claim SHOULD be paid by the accuser to the channel that was given the Strike within 10 days of the 10 day grace period for proving the claim ( this will see less and less false claims)
3. The person or company making the false strike should be then warned that this will not be tolerated and given THEIR first strike - reducing their ability to make a claim for 90 days.
- Future false claims then get the company banned from having the ability to do  Copyright Strike  for a period of time.
- If the company/ individuals continue these false strike claims, and have their own channel - this should then get banned for say 3 months, with an application for reinstatement required. With no revenue income from any current videos
- Further false Copyright Claims should mean the company / channel gets banned and ALL of their content removed

This is the only way I could see these false claims from happening - basically treat the accusers the same as the people currently getting false strikes made against them.

I got multiple strikes using Pretzel paid subscription for their "YouTube" friendly steam music - almost every video I put up got claimed despite me using a Chill Lo-fi paid subscription service with YouTube safe option turned on - each claim I protested and documented the right to use the music based on the Pretzel subscription and then the video was released - normally within the week. But again there was no financial recompense required from the accuser. 

As always Steve and @gamersNexus team, thank you for your awesome and informative content and thank you for fighting the fights we cant!

Author: @crazygazza07
Content:
At this point in time the fact YouTube does not look at overhauling the copyright system to help stop companies and persons abusing the system seems malicious.  While I am probably not the first person to suggest a system which may deter entities from abusing the system I think that maybe this could be a good middle ground.

1. When a claimant believes that have a genuine copyright claim against someone they submit their request they must place funds into a YouTube account with the amount determined by channel / company size and the amount of previous failed copyright claims.  The bigger the channel / company and the more failed / malicious claims the higher the amount needed.
2. The preliminary take down of the video of the upload happens however the creator will have the chance to respond to the claimant to argue about how there content falls under free use or other valid reason (not much of a change here).
3. If the claimant doesn't take the appropriate legal action because they truly believe they have a genuine case for copyright then the video is automatically restored after the expiry date.
4. At this point the create who has been damaged by the malicious claim can make monetary claim to YouTube with evidence of loss of income from loss of views.  The claimant publishing content related to the topic of the struck down video could be seen as re-direction of views and could be claimed while this maybe subjective as well.  But also could claim punitive damages for misuse of the copyright system could also be award however there would have to be certain metric that this would be based on.
5. A failed copyright claim will be placed on the claimant for future reference in the event of a future copyright claim.  Any funds that remain after the claim is settled will be returned to the claimant.

While maybe this isn't perfect I think it puts some actual financial stakes for those bigger companies who continue to bully creators who are just trying to enjoyable content for all of us.

Author: @Jules_Diplopia
Content:
Big companies are able to invest the time and effort to stretch out these kind of things.
Many years ago I suffered a fire that burnt out my printing business.  I was insured.  But the insurance company decided not to pay out and I had to take them to court.  It cost me 3 years and on the day that the case was due to be heard in court, my lawyer came up to me and said that the insurance company had "made an offer". He also made it plain that he strongly suggested that I accept.  
At that point, no longer certain that yourown lawyer was going to be working for you, knowing that you don't have the funds let alone the energy and time to go through all of this again, I caved and accepted. I think it was about 30% of the actual claim, and after the lawyers cut, far less.
But the point is that big companies like insurance companies or Media companies, have whole departments of expert lawyers, whos job is to stretch out such claims for as long as is possible, by whatever means they can. They assume that most plaintifs against them will give up.  They are right.  The system is rigged.

Author: @WhyOhWhyPhi
Content:
A bit of a story here:
So I'm a small reaction channel. Off and on over the last 7 years I've almost lost my channel 7 times due to copyright strikes. All of my work squarely falls under fair use. 
I would post some videos, get the usual copyright claim from BBC, fight it, LOSE (BBC is the only entity I've never won a dispute against at all) deal with it and move on. Then the occasional strike would roll in, video removed, etc etc. Each claim that's denied I could dispute that, but if you do, and they say "no it's in violation of copyright" you get a strike for it. 
So I stopped bothering to try. I just eat the demonetization. 

I would take the hit, keep uploading trying to learn as I went on what to do to avoid claims and strikes, when I would get 2 strikes I would have to stop uploading altogether for 90 days and sit in fear for 3 months praying I didn't get a 3rd since I'm too small for anyone to listen to me, or fight for me. Thankfully each time that tactic worked, but at the detriment of any momentum being squandered. 

Earlier this year I received 2 copyright strikes from the BBC from Season 2 of Doctor Who. These videos were released almost FIVE YEARS AGO! 
It was then that I said screw it, and removed every single reaction video from my channel. 
Letting a video sit in "unlisted" for a few days is pointless as they can hit you literally half a decade later if they decide to. 
I can't fight back for fear of losing my work completely. 

Since then I've been reuploading my reaction videos one by one, reworking them from the ground up with what I've learned over the past years in trying to get my clearly fair use videos past the broken system. The amount of editing I have to do to get them uploaded is insane. Everything from changing the pitch on some audio, to mirroring the footage, to adding a watermark over it, to having to mute audio completely. I've had footage as short as 3 seconds be hit for copyright.

My channel was never that large. But once I removed all of my videos I looked inconsistent so I lost subs. 
My main source of income was my Patreon. I've lost 90% of my Patreon subs in the last year due to this. 
I have medical/physical issues from a car accident years back. I can't do a regular job, my body can't handle it. Patreon was how I supported myself.
Any of that momentum is gone, my Patrons lost faith in me, and there's nothing I can do aside from what I'm doing now to try and rebuild things. 
But YT is a different beast than it was in 2019. My channel is now buried under a sea of other reaction channels. 

I'm still going, and I'm by no means complaining, but I wanted to share what it's like for a small creator who's been at the mercy of the broken system, has made numerous videos about it trying to stay transparent to my audience, and has been penalized over and over in various ways.

My analogy for the broken system YT uses has always been this:
BBC to YT: that person stole a candy bar from us
YT to Me: did you steal a candy bar from them?
Me to YT: no, this is my candy bar I worked for, it looks nothing like their candy bar. in fact what they say I stole is actually parts of MY candy bar.
YT to BBC: they say they didn't steal it, do you think they stole it?
BBC to YT: yes they stole it
YT to Me: they say you stole it so we're punishing you. 

The system has never made sense. A corporation can say you're violating fair use, even if you clearly aren't, and the solution is for YT to ask the people accusing you if you're doing it. OF COURSE they're going to say yes. It's the most a** backwards thing. 

Anyway sorry for the novel, thanks to anyone that read.

Content:
Hmmm, I am absolutely on your side. This mis-use of the fair-use licenses is stupid. The larger you are the more you can do in the US without being punished. :(
What I want to add from my perspective, if I may, when it comes to the YT strike system.
When I am developing my software I was aware, that internationally applied software is orientating itself at laws of the most strict country. In one case we take over rules from Singapure when it comes to money exchange laws etc. Since it is easily translatable to terms of logical constructs in a software; this funnily most often reflects the basic logic behind laws in other countries with deviations.
So my point is: I would consider the YT strike system even illegal from the EU point of view. So when YT is applying a strike for your video in the US, then so be it. But it should not be allowed to ban the video for EU viewers as well. This would at least grant you views and payments. So YT choose the most basic of all systems for cost measure reasons without considering further. In my career as developer I so often face the same approach, when the decision is made by people without the necessary skill for differentiation. "A club for a fly. Collateral damage expected and accepted." When the strike system would be country or region specific, it would be "nicer". Since Bloomberg has to make different contracts with major content providers in other regions in the world, this would, by any means, reflect reality in a better way.

I keep supporting you as best I can. Its torchlights like you, out there in the dark, who bring joy in form of warm sarcasm into at least my heart. 😊 Party On!!!🥳

Author: @BlairdBlaird
Content:
18:40 to be fair to youtube, IIRC they get several years worth of video uploaded *every hour*. Does not mean YT's algorithms are good but there there is no way to handle that volume non-algorithmically.

19:20 a bit debatable, reinstating the content after a counter-notice is required by law, I guess you could consider the strike removal siding with GN but at a very basic legal level it makes sense that if a counter-notification does not result in legal action the original notice was invalid, and thus so is the strike, so I would assume it's just part of the basic copyright strike workflow / automation. 

Not only that but it would not benefit large media companies to keep such strikes in place as they could get their own channels deleted (as hilarious as that would be). I would assume they do get copyright trolled all the time (though they likely have their own back channels to manage that more efficiently and with less damage).

Author: @DrakuzDark
Content:
1. DMCA Misrepresentation Claim (512(f))
The DMCA says if someone knowingly misrepresents that content is infringing, they’re liable for damages.
Case precedent: Lenz v. Universal (the “Dancing Baby” case). Court held copyright holders must consider fair use before issuing a takedown. If they don’t, that’s a misrepresentation.
For GN: Bloomberg would’ve had to intentionally ignore fair use (public speech + commentary). That’s a strong argument — it was a short excerpt of a public presidential speech, transformed in a documentary context.
Remedy: GN could sue for actual damages (lost revenue, costs) and possibly attorneys’ fees.

Author: @Gymnos2
Content: It's something every creator needs to be very careful of, especially with multiple videos. For example, my brother was doing voice over narrations for manga fan translations, he thought it was fair use and made a lot of uploads with no issue. One day, he found his account was completely gone -- from what I understood the Japanese publishing company DMCA'd all of his videos and each one earned him a copyright strike. He didn't even have a chance to fight it or delete the videos. I've personally seen my own share of ridiculous things as well, definitely not to the same devastating extent. For example, a certain indie developer's BGM was copyrighted, usually its not a problem for tutorials or gameplay videos, but in this case all 3 of his games music were flagged for copyright issues. Even when I tried to fight it as fair use, they disagreed and kept the restrictions leaving only one remaining route (legal). Deleted all my videos regarding his stuff and moved on, it was a real shame because this was such a small developer, you'd think they want all the videos of their games they could possibly get. Anyway just wanted to share, best of luck with your fight against false copyright claims!

Author: @chrisxd146
Content:
DMCA takedowns are the equivalent of SLAPP suits in that the intended outcome isn't a legal win, but silencing/suppressing the competition that can't afford to eat the legal costs. It got so bad that now 38 states have some kind of anti-SLAPP statute.

While it's convenient to blame YouTube as a company over their handling of the DMCA it's good to keep in mind that laws in the US don't keep up with the pace of modernization. False DMCA claims should have penalties ranging from 2x - 5x the damages inflicted as a hefty deterrent against abusing the system.

Author: @R3_dacted0
Content:
Copyright strikes should be time gated multiple ways.
1. A single strike should only be allowed to be filed and in effect at a time. 
2. It should be possible to bundle multiple applicable videos into a single claim, provided that each applicable video already exists on the channel at the time of filing. Only one claim can result in one strike, regardless of how many videos apply. 
3. If a channel is found in violation and given a strike, it should be immune to receiving a subsequent strike for any content they have already uploaded up until that point.

Separately, filing claims should also work on a strike system. Losing claims should result in strikes against you, ultimately resulting in you losing your ability to file claims after multiple attempts at creating false claims.

Author: @Deltarious
Content:
I've been through the process of learning in detail about YT's strike system several times at this point over more than 5 years by now and coincidentally Mr. French has been there each step of the way for me too, I see copyright on YT broadly the same as he does as a result. Having said that I want to point out that YT does not *fully* have free reign to just 'decide' how it's system works because there is a huge amount of grey area with how the DMCA and copyright law is specifically enforced and the companies *want* that grey area currently, to litigate it and establish a firm precident would potentially be disastrous and bring the fragile system down. As a result YT 'feels' a compulsion as a business to protect itself by erring on the side of claimants so that further action just never happens. So while yes, in principle they *could* come up with a more fair and just system they probably could not do so without either exposing themselves to more risk (even marginally so) *or* without spending more money on active moderation and policing, which would be the best outcome for probably everyone but that requires an effective monopoly to give up a fraction of their potential earnings so we know it's not likely to happen. 

What's that, you say? Generating positive creator sentiment by increasing confidence in the moderation system may, over the long run, result in increased profits due to that in turn increasing trust, content quality and then user sentiment/engagement and thus watch time? Don't be silly, we aren't allowed to be forward thinking when it comes to profit! 

Oh and as a P.S: Shout out to Tom Scott who probably has the most concise but highly informative coverage of the topic, his video leaves out some of the finer nuance for time but is absolutely fantastic for anyone asking 'why does YouTube's claim system work that way?'

Since 2022, the U.S. Copyright Office runs an optional small-claims-like forum called the CCB.

It handles copyright infringement or misrepresentation claims for up to $30,000 in damages, with streamlined procedures and optional participation.

If you believe someone knowingly filed a false DMCA takedown notice (e.g., targeting fair-use content), the CCB can hear a §512(f) misrepresentation claim.

Participation is voluntary: the other party can opt out, in which case you’d need to file in federal court.
